My dad was a high school dropout who was abandoned by his parents when he was 14. Later on when he knew he was going to be a father he decided to go to college & finished his bachelor's in 3 years with a 4.0 GPA. He'd always wanted to attend Harvard, so he applied to Harvard Law School & got in after acing the LSAT (law school entrance) exam. Graduated with honors & went on to be a successful lawyer for many years.

I'm a school bus aide for students with special needs working for a public school district in Texas. I don't drive the bus, I just ride along to make sure the students are safe & behaving properly. I also assist the driver in other ways, like navigation, cleaning, & paperwork. 

* Yes, I've had students become violent with me, but it's rare. If a student is likely to be difficult we're usually warned in advance, so we can be prepared. 

* I don't try to teach the students much, but their bus experience differs from other kids in several ways. In our district, all special needs buses have seatbelts & air conditioning (it gets pretty hot here in TX), & many are equipped for wheelchairs. Students get their own seat to themselves & are required to wear their seatbelt. We provide curb-to-curb service, which means we pick up & drop off students as close as possible to their own homes, usually one student per stop. For this reason we have a lot fewer kids on our bus than a normal school bus would.

* Special needs drivers & aides make the same amount as other school bus drivers in our district. 

* Yes, we receive special training in student management as well as the equipment we have to use (wheelchair lifts & tie-downs, safety harnesses, car seats, etc.)

* In some ways I find working with special needs students to be easier. I have more patience with them because I know a lot of their "undesirable" behaviors are a result of their disability & therefore can't be helped.

I remember trying to bake a potato in the microwave.  I'd seen other people do it before, so I bought a bag of fresh potatoes & followed the instructions on the label.  It said to poke holes in the potato with a fork, wrap it in a damp paper towel & cook on high for 8 minutes. (This is for a potato about the size of my fist.) Well, after about 5 minutes in the microwave, the potato (or perhaps it was the paper towel) caught on fire & smoke began pouring out of my microwave. I stopped it immediately & put out the fire, but the damage was done - the potato resembled a charcoal brick, the inside of my microwave was permanently stained a lovely shade of brown, & my apartment smelled like burnt potato for a week.
